title: Question words
plainEnglish: 누구, 어디, 언제, 뭐, 왜, 어떻게 turn a sentence into an open question.
whenToUse: Use these when a yes/no answer is not enough and you need one missing detail.
attachmentRule: Put the question word where the answer would normally appear: 누가 왔어요?, 어디에 가요?, 왜 못 가요?
contrastWith: A plain rising tone makes a yes/no question. A question word asks for specific missing information.
commonMistakes: Do not place every question word at the front as if it were English.
Do not answer 왜 with a place or 어디 with a reason.
beginnerExplanation: Korean question words usually stay inside the normal sentence slot. If the missing answer is a person, use 누구/누가; if it is a place, use 어디; if it is a reason, use 왜.
studyOrder: Pick the missing information.
Choose the matching Korean question word.
Place it in the answer slot.
Keep the ending polite unless the context is casual.

title: Speech levels
plainEnglish: Korean endings change by situation: 해요체 for everyday politeness, 합쇼체 for formal settings, and 반말 only with close permission.
whenToUse: Use 해요체 as the safe default for adult everyday speech. Use formal forms for announcements, service, interviews, and presentations.
attachmentRule: Keep the same stem and change the ending/register: 가요, 갑니다, 가.
contrastWith: Honorific 시 respects the person in the sentence; speech level manages your relationship with the listener.
commonMistakes: Do not switch to 반말 just because the sentence is short.
Do not use formal 합쇼체 everywhere; it can sound stiff in close everyday talk.
beginnerExplanation: Speech level is not just grammar decoration; it tells the listener how formal, close, or careful the situation is. When unsure, 해요체 is the safest spoken default.
studyOrder: Identify the listener.
Choose safe politeness first.
Add honorific 시 only when the subject needs respect.
Check whether the situation is casual, service, or formal.

title: Possession / genitive
plainEnglish: Use 의 to mark possession or a noun-to-noun relationship, especially in written or careful Korean.
whenToUse: Use 의 for my/your/someone's things, institutional names, and careful noun phrases.
attachmentRule: Attach 의 after the owner or first noun: 친구의 가방, 한국의 날씨.
contrastWith: In fast spoken Korean, 의 is often dropped or pronounced like 에, but written Korean usually keeps it.
commonMistakes: Do not attach 의 after the possessed noun.
Do not overuse 의 in every spoken noun phrase when natural Korean would omit it.
beginnerExplanation: 의 links two nouns. The first noun owns, labels, or narrows the second noun. 제 is the common reduced form for 저의.
studyOrder: Find the owner or first noun.
Attach 의 to that noun.
Put the main noun after it.
Decide whether spoken Korean would naturally shorten it.

title: The copula 이다
plainEnglish: 이다 turns a noun into a sentence and changes shape in past, reason, background, and contrast clauses.
whenToUse: Use 이다 when the predicate is a noun: student, doctor, plan, problem, reason.
attachmentRule: After consonants use 이에요, after vowels often use 예요. In clauses it becomes 이라서, 이고, 이면, 이었어요/였어요.
contrastWith: Adjectives and verbs do not need 이다. 학생이에요 is right, but 가다이에요 is not.

examples.en: Because they are my friend, I helped.

commonMistakes: Do not add 이다 after a verb stem.
Do not forget the noun-final consonant/vowel split for 이에요/예요.
beginnerExplanation: 이다 is the noun sentence-maker. If the last meaningful word is a noun, Korean needs a copula shape to finish the sentence.
studyOrder: Check whether the predicate is a noun.
Choose 이에요/예요 in polite speech.
Change 이다 when connecting clauses.
Do not attach it to action verbs.

title: Volition, inference, and softening with 겠
plainEnglish: 겠 can show the speaker will do something, infer something from evidence, or soften formal speech.
whenToUse: Use 겠 for formal willingness, careful guesses, empathy, and service-style polite statements.
attachmentRule: Attach 겠 to a verb or adjective stem before the final ending: 하겠습니다, 맛있겠어요, 힘드시겠어요.
contrastWith: Plain future -(으)ㄹ 거예요 predicts or plans. 겠 often sounds more formal, inferential, or service-oriented.

examples.en: It looks like it will rain.
That must be very hard for you.

commonMistakes: Do not treat 겠 as the only future tense.
Do not use service-style 겠 forms in every casual sentence.
beginnerExplanation: 겠 is a control knob for stance. It can mean 'I will', 'it looks like', or 'that must be', depending on who controls the action and what evidence the speaker has.
studyOrder: Decide whether this is will, guess, or empathy.
Attach 겠 to the stem.
Choose the right politeness ending.
Compare with -(으)ㄹ 거예요 before using it as future.

title: Unreal conditionals
plainEnglish: Use past conditional frames to talk about unreal results, regrets, and imagined alternatives.
whenToUse: Use this when the condition did not happen and you are imagining a different result.
attachmentRule: Attach 았/었더라면 to the past stem, then state the imagined result with -(으)ㄹ 텐데요 or -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
contrastWith: Plain -(으)면 can be real or future. -았/었더라면 strongly points to an unreal past condition.

examples.en: If I had come early, I would have met them.
If I had had time, I would have gone.
It would have been good if I had studied.

commonMistakes: Do not use this for a simple future condition.
Do not forget that the condition is already unreal or regretted.

practiceItems.prompt: Say: If I had known, I would have gone.
Say: If I had time, I would have helped.

beginnerExplanation: This form is for a path that did not happen. It often carries regret, relief, or reflection about a different possible outcome.
studyOrder: Confirm the condition did not happen.
Make the condition past.
Attach 더라면 or use 있었다면/이었다면.
Make the result imagined, not factual.

title: Nominalisation contrast
plainEnglish: 기 names an action as an abstract activity; 는 것 packages a more specific event or fact.
whenToUse: Use 기 for general activities and evaluation. Use 는 것 when describing an event, fact, habit, or thing someone does.
attachmentRule: Attach 기 directly to the verb stem. For 는 것, use the present modifier before 것.
contrastWith: 기 is compact and activity-like; 는 것 is heavier and more event-like.

examples.en: I didn't know that it was late.

commonMistakes: Do not use 기 for every English gerund.
Do not forget 것 when packaging a full clause as a noun.
beginnerExplanation: Both forms let a verb behave like a noun. 기 feels like naming an activity; 는 것 feels like pointing to a specific thing, fact, or event.
studyOrder: Ask whether you mean an activity or a fact/event.
Use 기 for activity labels.
Use 는 것 for packaged clauses.
Check the particle after the nominalized phrase.

title: Formal written connectors
plainEnglish: Formal Korean writing uses connectors like 따라서, 그러나, 반면에, 즉, and 결국 to organise argument flow.
whenToUse: Use these in essays, notices, reports, news-style writing, and structured explanations.
attachmentRule: Use them at the beginning of the next sentence or clause to show the relationship to the previous idea.
contrastWith: Spoken connectors like 그래서 and 근데 are natural in conversation but often too casual for formal writing.

examples.romanization: biga watseumnida. ttaraseo gyeonggiga chwiso dwaetseumnida.
examples.en: It rained. Therefore, the game was canceled.
The price is high. However, the quality is good.
In other words, we need to check again.

commonMistakes: Do not mix very casual endings with formal written connectors.
Do not use 따라서 when the second sentence is not a result.

practiceItems.prompt: Connect: It snowed. Therefore, school is closed.
Start a contrast sentence with 그러나.

beginnerExplanation: These words are road signs for written logic. They tell the reader whether the next sentence is a result, contrast, summary, or conclusion.
studyOrder: Name the logic relation.
Choose the connector.
Keep the sentence ending formal enough.
Check whether the previous sentence really supports the connector.

title: Internet language and intensifiers
plainEnglish: Korean digital language uses consonant emoticons, shortenings, and casual intensifiers that must stay in informal contexts.
whenToUse: Use these in chats with friends, comments, memes, or casual texting, not in formal writing.
attachmentRule: Place them like tone markers around short casual sentences: ㅋㅋ, ㅠㅠ, 진짜, 완전, 대박.
contrastWith: Polite email, school writing, workplace notices, and customer messages need standard vocabulary instead.
commonMistakes: Do not use ㅋㅋ or ㅠㅠ in formal assignments or business messages.
Do not assume every internet expression is safe with older or unfamiliar listeners.

practiceItems.prompt: Make a casual chat reaction: That's amazing.

beginnerExplanation: Internet Korean is mostly about register. The words may be simple, but the social setting matters more than the literal meaning.
studyOrder: Identify the channel.
Check your relationship with the reader.
Choose casual or standard wording.
Remove internet markers before formal writing.

title: Integrated production checklist
plainEnglish: Before producing Korean, check purpose, listener, register, particles, verb shape, tense, connector, and closing.
whenToUse: Use this before a final speaking or writing task, especially when combining several grammar points.
attachmentRule: Run the checks in order: purpose, listener, register, sentence core, particles, tense, connector, ending.
contrastWith: Do not only translate English word by word. Korean output needs sentence role, listener relationship, and ending choice.

examples.ko: 저는 내일 회의에 갈 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun naeil hoeuie gal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can go to the meeting tomorrow.

examples.ko: 비가 와서 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: biga waseo jogeum neujeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: I think I will be a little late because it is raining.

commonMistakes: Do not stop checking after vocabulary is correct.
Do not mix casual slang with formal closings unless the task asks for register contrast.

practiceItems.prompt: Say one polite sentence about tomorrow's plan.

beginnerExplanation: This card is a final quality gate. It helps you catch the things learners miss after they already know the words: particles, endings, tense, connectors, and social tone.
studyOrder: State the communicative purpose.
Choose the listener/register.
Build the Korean sentence core.
Check particles and endings.
Read it aloud once before submitting.

title: Tensification
plainEnglish: Some consonants become tense after blocked final consonants, so written Korean and spoken Korean may differ.
whenToUse: Use this when a following consonant sounds stronger than its spelling after a 받침.
attachmentRule: Notice the 받침 before ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, or ㅈ; the next sound may tighten in pronunciation.
contrastWith: Liaison carries a final consonant into a vowel. Tensification strengthens the next consonant instead.

examples.en: rice soup, often pronounced with a tense pp sound
school, often pronounced with a tense kk sound
to read, often pronounced with a tense tt sound

commonMistakes: Do not expect spelling and sound to match perfectly.
Do not add an extra vowel between the two consonants.

practiceItems.prompt: Read 국밥 with the common tense sound.
Read 학교 with the common tense sound.

beginnerExplanation: Korean spelling keeps word history visible, but speech often tightens the next consonant after a final consonant. Recognising the pattern makes listening less surprising.
studyOrder: Find the 받침.
Look at the next consonant.
Listen for a tighter sound.
Keep the original spelling when writing.
